title: Snowflake API: Which One to Use? (2026 Guide)
summary: The Snowflake API includes multiple REST interfaces with different endpoints, limits, and error codes. Determine which one fits your integration needs.
body_markdown:
## Run Snowflake queries from workflows with Activepieces


Activepieces suits Snowflake work that a schedule or an event starts, such as a weekly query or a row-triggered lookup, and a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has. It handles the retry and error-branch plumbing so your own code doesn't have to.


### When a workflow tool is the right layer


Start with ownership: every Activepieces flow that touches Snowflake runs under one stored connection, and that connection holds one Snowflake user's private key or token.


On a self-hosted instance or the enterprise cloud tier, that secret can sit in your own secret manager instead of the Activepieces database, so no vendor, us included, ever holds the key to your Snowflake user.


Point a self-hosted instance at an external secret manager and the key is simply absent from its database; secret managers are listed in the enterprise feature set alongside SCIM, custom RBAC and audit logs.


Name that user, record its role, and give it only the grants the flow needs. If the answer is "whoever built the flow", the flow will break the day that person leaves.


### Two routes to Snowflake


Activepieces has two routes. Its Snowflake integration is one of 750 in the open source monorepo, so the current action list can be read in` packages/pieces/community` rather than taken from a description; plan around that list.


Where it falls short, an HTTP step can call the SQL API with a bearer token, and for key pair authentication you sign the JWT yourself and pass it in the header.


Because statements may complete asynchronously, the flow should submit, then poll or branch on status, rather than assume a result came back.


### Retry and error rules in the builder


The builder is where the retry and error rules live. The screenshot shows a four-step flow: a weekly schedule trigger, "Find Rows" and "Add Row" steps on Google Sheets, and an "Ask AI" step.


The highlighted Find Rows step has its panel open, with a search value of` {{step_2\['output'\]}}` . This shows one step's output feeding the next, and an error handling section sits at the bottom of the panel.


Treat that pattern as your template: each Snowflake step takes a reference from the step before it, and each has its own failure setting, so a failed statement can route to an alert instead of silently stopping the run.


### Idempotent Snowflake API retries in workflows


That reuse of output is also why idempotency matters here. A retried step with an INSERT needs the request identifier from the previous section, or the retry duplicates rows.


### When native Snowflake tasks are better


Once the work is heavy transformation, continuous file ingestion or a dependency graph of models, move it inside Snowflake.


Tasks run scheduled SQL under Snowflake's own roles and warehouses, Snowpipe loads files as they arrive, and dbt manages model dependencies and tests. Each keeps data and credentials inside the platform, so there's no external connection to own, rotate or audit.


Use Activepieces to notify, trigger or reconcile around those jobs, not to replace them. Its core is MIT-licensed, so a security review can clone the repository, read the queue and worker architecture, and run it self-hosted or air-gapped before any Snowflake credential goes near it.
